words.note: packet maps to pie-root-wekw-speak; vácas- is the s-stem *wékʷos exactly

cognate: Ved. √śru- (śr̥ṇavat, śrāváya, śr̥ṇviṣe) = Gk κλύω (ἔκλυες, ἔκλυε) < *ḱlew-; Ved. vácas- (neuter s-stem) = Gk ἔπος < *wékʷos, with the root noun vā́c- (*wṓkʷs) as variant object in RV 8.96.12d; 1sg possessive Ved. me (enclitic gen.) ~ Gk ἐμόν.
drift_or_renewal: none in the core pair; Vedic alternates vácas-/vā́c-/háva- as object, Greek alternates ἔπος with the bare genitive of the praying person (ἔκλυες εὐξαμένοιο). The worshipper is named by an agent noun of a praise/prayer root in both (Ved. stotúḥ 'of the praiser', Gk εὐξαμένοιο 'of (me) praying'), non-cognate.
shared_syntax: verb of hearing + object 'word' (+ possessive/genitive of the speaker): Ved. stotúḥ ... vácaḥ śr̥ṇavat ... me / śr̥ṇavat vácāṃsi me; Gk ἐμὸν ἔπος ἔκλυες εὐξαμένοιο. Subject = the deity, object = the worshipper's utterance.
context: Both are prayer language: the god is asked to hear, or reminded that he once heard, the worshipper's word. AVŚ 6.2.1 is an invocation of Indra at the Soma pressing ('who shall hear the praiser's word and my call'); Il. 16.236 (= 14.234) is Achilles' prayer to Zeus ('you heard my word when I prayed before, so now too...'); Il. 10.295 is the narrative closing of a prayer ('so they spoke praying, and Pallas Athena heard them'), matching RV 7.8.5c 'praised, Agni, you are heard/you listen' and RV 1.54.2b 'praise Indra who listens'. The same speech-act frame (deity as hearer of the poet's word) and the same s-stem *wékʷos make a generic 'hear a word' unlikely to be the whole story; in both traditions *wékʷos is the marked word for the poet's/worshipper's formal utterance.
phrase: *ḱlew- (aor./subj.) + *wékʷos (acc.) + *me/*h₁eme- 'hear my word' (god as subject, in prayer)

words.note: packet mapping to *leǵ- is wrong: εἶπον < *we-wkʷ-; lemma: corpus lemma; actually εἶπον

cognate: Gk ἔργον / ἔρδω (*wérǵom / *wr̥ǵ-yé-) = OE weorc (*wérǵom) = Av. (hu-)varšta- (*werǵ-); Gk ἔπος / εἶπον (*wékʷos / *we-wkʷ-) = Av. (h)ūxta- (*ukʷ-to-, *wekʷ-).
drift_or_renewal: Germanic renews the 'word' member with *werdʰom (OE word, cognate Lat. uerbum), keeping *wérǵom; Aeschylus renews 'speak' with λέγω (ἔρδειν καὶ λέγειν). Plausible because *wekʷ- 'speak' was lost as a verb in Germanic, while 'word' was needed as the paired noun.
shared_syntax: coordinated merism of two nouns (or verbs) 'word and deed', in either order, often with a conjunction pair (Gk ἢ ... ἠέ / τε ... τε; OE and; Av. -ca ... -ca), used as a totalizing expression of conduct.
context: All anchors use the pair to sum up a person's whole conduct: Hes. Op. 710 offence 'by saying a word or by doing', Theognis 307 'learned base deeds and words', Beo. 289 the coast-guard who must judge 'words and works', Crist 'with words and works they did his will'. Same ethical/legal summarizing function as Av. humata- hūxta- huuaršta- 'good thought, word, deed'. Merisms of this kind are widespread, so the weight lies in the double cognation (*wekʷ- and *werǵ-) shared by Greek and Avestan and the single (*werǵ-) one in Germanic.

cognate: In the wider formula: Lat. pecua = Umbr. pequo = Av. pasu = Ved. paśu- (*péḱu); Umbr. ueiro = Av. vīra- = Ved. vīrá- (*wiHro-). In the packet itself: Lat. domo (*dóm-) ~ Av. nmāne (*dm-) 'in/for the house' as the locus of the blessing; Lat. salua seruassis = Umbr. salua seritu (exact Italic cognate pair).
drift_or_renewal: Cato renews *wiHro- with pastores 'herdsmen' (Umbrian keeps ueiro); the Avestan Shnuman passage renews *peḱu with gav- 'cattle' (gə̄ušca vąθβa 'herds of cattle') beside vīra-, and AVP 19.53.35 spreads the pair into gavām aśvānāṃ puruṣāṇāṃ. Renewal of one member while the dyad and its function persist is exactly what is expected of a fixed merism.
shared_syntax: dyad 'men and cattle' (asyndetic or with -que/-ca) as object of a protective/blessing wish addressed to a god, with the household as beneficiary: Lat. pastores pecuaque salua seruassis ... mihi domo familiaeque; Av. buiiāt̰ aɱi nmāne gə̄ušca vąθβa upa vīranąmca 'may there be in this house herds of cattle and of men'; Ved. adhipatiṃ mā kṛṇu gavām ... puruṣāṇāṃ.
context: All three are ritual speech asking a god for the welfare of a household's people and livestock: Cato's lustration prayer to Mars pater (passage and its next sentence), the Avestan Fravashi hymn's blessing on the worshipper's house, and the AVP formula asking Agni/Soma to make the speaker lord over cows, horses and men. The merism is not generic vocabulary but the core of a known Italic-Iranian-Indic prayer formula (the Umbrian Iguvine 'nerf arsmo ueiro pequo castruo fri salua seritu' is its closest twin to Cato).
phrase: *wiHro- *peḱu (+ *dem- 'house') as object of a prayer for protection: 'keep safe men and cattle (of my house)'

words.note: packet etymon rejected: Osc. famel; packet's *dʰeh₁- mapping is wrong

cognate: Ved. paśu- = Lat. pecus (*péḱu); Ved. vīrá- = Lat. uir (*wiHro-), the latter present in Cato 149.2 only in the legal phrase uiri boni arbitratu, not inside the dyad.
drift_or_renewal: Latin fills the 'men' slot with pastores (herdsmen) or familia (the household's slaves) instead of *uiri, as Cato also does in his lustration prayer (pastores pecuaque, 141.3); Umbrian keeps ueiro pequo. Vedic keeps both members (paśavaḥ ... vīrāḥ; paśubhiś ca vīraiḥ).
shared_syntax: coordinated dyad 'livestock and men' denoting the movable possessions/dependants of a household: Ved. paśavo 'smākaṃ prajā asmākaṃ vīrā asmākam; Lat. si quid emptor aut pastores aut pecus emptoris ... damni dederit; pecus et familia ... pigneri sunto.
context: Both passages inventory what belongs to a party: the AVŚ 16.8 curse lists what is 'ours' (victory, truth, brahman, cattle, offspring, men) before excluding the enemy; Cato's lease-contract lists the buyer's herdsmen and livestock as liable for damage and pledges 'livestock and household'. The AVP 19.56 anchor is the refrain hymn whose neighbouring verses end 'with cattle and men' (paśubhiś ca vīraiḥ). This is the same *wiHro- *peḱu dyad as in Italic and Avestan prayer formulae, here in its possessive/legal use.
phrase: *wiHro- + *peḱu 'men and livestock' (a household's dependants and herds)

words.note: packet etymon rejected: οὐρανός etymology disputed

cognate: Ved. sū́rya- = Gk ἥλιος (*sh₂wél-/*sóh₂wl̥); Ved. gam- (agamat) = Gk βαίνω (ἀμφιβέβηκε) < *gʷem-.
drift_or_renewal: 'sky' renewed in Greek: οὐρανόν for *dyéwm̥ (Ved. divam/dyām); the preverb 'around' renewed (Ved. pári in AVŚ 6.12.1, Gk ἀμφί), not cognate.
shared_syntax: sun (subject) + *gʷem- (past: aor. agamat / plpf. ἀμφιβεβήκει) + accusative of the sky as goal/space traversed; AVŚ 6.12.1 adds 'around' (pári dyā́m ... sū́ryaḥ ... agamam) like Gk ἀμφί-.
context: Both describe the sun's course across the sky as a stepping/going: AVP 19.36.26 (context line) 'the king has gone to his seat, the sun has gone to heaven'; Il. 8.68 (= 16.777) a time formula 'when the Sun had stepped around mid-heaven'. Sun's motion is a natural topic, and *gʷem- is a common verb, so the parallel could be independent; it is the agreement in verb root plus accusative of the sky that makes it worth noting.

cognate: Ved. stanayanti = Gk στενάχουσι, both 3pl present of *(s)tenh₂- 'roar, thunder'.
drift_or_renewal: Greek στένω/στενάχω is mostly 'groan, lament' of persons (as in most Greek anchors of this packet), but Homer regularly uses it of the sea and the earth (Il. 23.230, 2.781, 2.784, 2.95), i.e. the 'roar' sense that Vedic has for thunder is alive in Greek nature description; no drift is claimed here. The subject differs slightly: Vedic says the rains thunder (from the cloud) in a simile for the roaring river Sindhu, Greek says the storm-torrents roar as they flow into the sea.
shared_syntax: plural subject (rain/torrents) + 3pl present *(s)tenh₂- with a directional complement (Ved. abhrā́t ... prá 'forth from the cloud'; Gk ἐς ἅλα 'into the sea'), inside a comparison.
context: Both are images of water in spate in a rainstorm: RV 10.75.3 (river hymn) 'her roar rises to heaven above the earth ... as from the cloud the rains thunder forth, when the Sindhu comes bellowing like a bull'; Il. 16.384-392 storm simile where Zeus pours down rain and the torrents rush 'roaring loudly into the purple sea'. The same root, in the same tense and number, for the noise of rain-swollen water, inside a simile, in both; the image itself is natural, so the case rests on root identity plus the specific rainstorm-flood frame.

cognate: Ved. tanyatú-/stanáyati = Lat. tonitrus/tonāre (*(s)tenh₂-); with the sky god Ved. Dyaús (dyóḥ, diváḥ) ~ Lat. Iuppiter/Iou- (*dyew-) and Gk Ζεύς (Διί, support).
drift_or_renewal: Latin in the anchors renews *dyew- 'sky' with caelum (tonitru ... caeli) or leaves the thunderer implicit (Plautus: Jupiter's thunder in the Amphitruo, tonuit ... di); Cicero's augural 'Iove tonante' (Div. 2.42; recalled, not in the local corpus) keeps *dyew-. Greek replaced the thunder verb (βροντάω) and uses *(s)tenh₂- only for the earth's response to Zeus's thunderbolt (Hes. Th. 858; Il. 2.781 γαῖα ὑπεστενάχιζε Διί).
shared_syntax: genitive or subject *dyew- + *(s)tenh₂- noun/verb: Ved. tanyatóḥ ... dyóḥ 'the thunder of Dyaus', stanáyan iva dyaúḥ 'thundering like Dyaus'; Lat. Iove tonante, tonitru caeli.
context: Weather-god thunder in both: the Vedic similes compare a god's roar to the thundering of Dyaus/heaven; Latin attributes thunder to Jupiter/the sky. The collocation 'sky thunders' is natural and could arise anywhere; what favours inheritance is that the god-name *dyew- (not only a word for 'sky') is the thunderer in Indic and Italic, and that Greek attests the root beside Zeus. I would not press it beyond a low rating.
